name: Nestle permanent wave machine

card.summary: Karl Nessler's early electric perm apparatus used heated brass rollers to give long hair lasting waves and curls.
card.aka: Eugene Nessler wave machine, Nessler spiral heat method
card.note: Historical device; hot rollers and caustic solution caused burns in early use.

quick.overview:
The Nessler machine was an early way to give hair permanent waves. Hair was wrapped around heated rods and treated with an alkaline solution so it set in a curl that lasted months, unlike temporary styling.

It matters to hair-style history as the forerunner of the modern perm, a way to add texture and volume. It was slow, hot and dangerous by today's standards.
quick.how: Salons of the era wrapped long hair spirally around about twelve heated brass rollers with counterweights hung from an overhead frame, a process of about six hours [1].
quick.risks: The rollers reached 100 degrees Celsius or more and early trials burned hair and scalp [1]. The machine is a historical item, replaced by chemical perms.

lead: Karl Nessler, a German hairdresser later known in Britain and the US as Charles Nestle, developed an electric permanent wave method, with its first public demonstration on 8 October 1905 [1].

The 'spiral heat method' wrapped long hair around rods heated to 100 degrees Celsius or more, with caustic soda applied, and took roughly six hours. Counterweights hung from an overhead chandelier kept the roughly 2-pound brass rollers off the scalp [1].

He tested it on his wife, whose hair was burned off in the first two attempts before the method was refined. It was used in London in 1909, and Nessler later sold a home-use machine and operated under the Nestle name [1].

chain: Hair wrapped on heated rods with alkaline solution
angle.text: The machine produced permanent waves, giving long hair lasting curl without nightly setting.

paras: Wig-setting solutions before Nessler were considered too harsh for skin [1]. Nessler moved to London in 1901, was jailed as a German in World War I, and escaped to New York in 1915 [1].

timeline.event: Used in London on long hair [1]
